column4: The powerful jinn says he will bring the throne before Solomon rises, giving a concrete Quranic scene for the section's secondary sense of ءتى as bringing rather than giving.
The person with knowledge brings the throne before Solomon's glance returns, intensifying the bringing sense introduced in 27:39 and distinguishing it from monetary giving.
God gives and removes dominion, honors and abases, and all good is in His hand; giving, taking, benefit, and the hand meet explicitly here.
People must spend from that over which God made them successors, so the human giver is a trustee of a prior gift rather than an original benefactor who can claim mastery.
The seed multiplied seven hundredfold depicts God, rather than the human recipient, supplying the increase returned for expenditure.
Open charity is good but concealed charity to the poor is better and removes sins, protecting the gift from display and from social leverage over its recipient.
Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, have their reward with their Lord, placing recompense outside the beneficiary's debt.
God is the one who accepts charities, identifying the ultimate receiver of a gift whose needy human recipient is not made liable for repayment.
Creditors who abandon usury retain only their principal and must neither wrong nor be wronged, setting the boundary immediately before the hardship rule of 2:280.
The Israelites ransom captives while also expelling and attacking their own people; the verse exposes the contradiction between an unbinding payment and conduct that recreates subjection.
Feeding on a day of hunger continues the steep ascent whose first definition in 90:13 is freeing a neck, joining emancipation to an opened provision hand.
The orphaned relative is the first specified recipient of the feeding in 90:14, distinguishing this ayah's contribution from the act and from the next recipient.
The destitute person in the dust is the second specified recipient, completing the passage's movement from freeing a slave to relieving acute need.
Israel is commanded to remember God's favor, beginning an account in which the next verses identify liberation from Pharaoh as the content of that favor.
God's rescue of Israel from Pharaoh's household and its brutal oppression specifies the emancipating favor recalled in 2:47.
Moses says that God favored Israel above others, naming the true benefactor immediately before another retelling of their release from Pharaoh.
Rescue from Pharaoh's people and their killing of sons supplies the concrete liberation behind the favor named in 7:140.
The condemned person says that his wealth did not avail him, a direct parallel to the section's wealth failing its owner at the fall.
The person who gathers wealth and repeatedly counts it embodies the grasping hand that converts possession into a continuing account.
His belief that wealth will make him immortal states the false security behind the accumulation in 104:2 and the wealth that cannot save in the section.
Every favor possessed by people is declared to be from God, displacing the human benefactor's claim to be the originating hand.
No one can withhold mercy God opens and no one can release what He withholds, placing the open and closed hand ultimately under divine rule.
The question who could provide if God withheld His provision exposes the human hand's dependence on a prior divine opening.
The command to do good as God has done good to the addressee turns received benefit into onward beneficence rather than a claim against recipients.
Evil is recompensed only with its like while righteous action receives entry into provision without account, another explicit boundary between the two directions of recompense.
One who brings good receives better than it, whereas evil is repaid only according to the deed, contrasting generous and equivalent forms of divine recompense.
The question about a garden destroyed when its elderly owner and dependents most need it continues the spending passage with another image of worldly provision suddenly leaving the hand empty.
Believers are ordered to relinquish outstanding usury, naming the creditor's surrender of excess immediately before 2:279 limits collection to principal.
The command to record a deferred debt and its term supplies the ordinary creditor-debtor world from which charitable remission and divine repayment depart.
The command to do good includes those whom one's right hands possess, requiring beneficence precisely within the master-dependent relation developed by the section.
Secret counsel is good when it commands charity or reconciliation, and seeking God's approval moves its great reward away from human beneficiaries.
Captives are promised that God may give them better than what was taken from them, reversing loss and custody through divine giving.
The distribution rule prevents public wealth from circulating only among the rich, limiting the use of the giving hand to consolidate dependency and power.
The boast of having consumed abundant wealth presents expenditure as self-display, a plausible counter-image to giving solely for God's face.
The command not to oppress the orphan precedes the command about the asker, extending restraint from the refusing hand to another dependent person.
Driving away the orphan supplies the bodily rejection whose next verse becomes refusal to encourage feeding the poor.
God as the believers' protecting ally brings them from darkness to light, supplying a liberating act for the section's benefactor-patron branch of ولى.
God, rather than hostile human powers, is the believers' patron and the best helper, another direct Quranic location of true mawlāship.
If opponents turn away, believers are reminded that God is their patron, the best patron and helper, joining تولي with the true source of protection.
Every person's record is fastened to the neck, bringing the section's debt garment and neck-bound withheld wealth into the scene of final accounting.
The person must read his own record and suffice as accountant, specifying the collection and reckoning implied by the neck-bound record of 17:13.
After the garden owner's empty-handed regret, no party can help him against God and he cannot defend himself, removing the human patronage on which worldly benefit might rely.
The ruined-garden scene concludes that true protection belongs to God and that He gives the better reward and outcome, relocating both patronage and recompense.
The condemned person's authority has vanished, completing 69:28's failed wealth with the collapse of the power that wealth was supposed to secure.
The accumulator is thrown into the Crusher, completing the reversal in which gathered wealth cannot prevent the owner's fall.
Moses asks Israel to remember God's favor in making them a free, endowed people, another divine-benefaction frame for the community rescued from servitude.
People recognize God's favor and then deny it, a specific failure to acknowledge the originating giver rather than a debt owed to a human intermediary.
Whatever good people send ahead they will find with God, locating the retained value of generosity in divine keeping instead of the recipient's obligation.
A greeting must be answered with one better or equal, providing a bounded form of human reciprocity that clarifies what the section's uncollectable gift leaves behind.
Everyone in the heavens and earth comes to the Merciful as a servant, joining the root's coming sense to the section's slave relation in one eschatological scene.
Each person comes to God alone, completing 19:93 by stripping the arriving servant of every human patron and account.
